newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis doubt coup warning but are nervous.
newsitem.headline: Israelis doubt coup warning but are nervous.

text.p: Most Israelis on Thursday dismissed a warning of an army takeover but were clearly rattled by the suggestion that conditions for a coup existed.

Politicians from left and right scoffed at the assessment that tension between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's four-month-old government and top brass could lead disgruntled officers to stage a coup.
Retired generals said it would never happen in the Jewish state, and one editorial writer said it was irresponsible.
But the mere assertion and the public debate it spawned may have been enough to shatter a national myth and drag Israel unwillingly past another social watershed.
"This is a milestone. From the moment the remark was made, no one can ignore the warning. No one can say this possibility was not taken into account," said Amnon Barzilai of the Haaretz newspaper.
It was Barzilai who set off the storm on Wednesday by publishing an interview with Professor Zeev Maoz, head of the Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies.
Maoz, whose privately-funded centre is one of Israel's leading think tanks, said senior officers felt Netanyahu had usurped their role in decision-making and given it to his own political advisers.

"The military has no opportunity to play the political game in order to change the situation and therefore the likelihood of a putsch -- an illegal action -- becomes more and more attractive," said Maoz.

Officers in the army's general staff, including army chief Amnon Shahak, played key negotiating roles in the previous Labour government's peace deals with the PLO that sprouted from the breakthrough 1993 Oslo agreement.

Netanyahu, who opposed the deals and ousted Labour in elections last May, has criticised the generals' involvement in the talks. People close to the prime minister talk about "Oslo officers" who are politically tainted.

Likud legislator Uzi Landau, who heads the Knesset's powerful Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, referred to members of the general staff earlier this year as "lackeys" of the previous government.
Military analyst Ron Ben-Ishai wrote this week that Netanyahu "does not trust some top security and intelligence officials and does not share his thoughts or his plans with them."
Israel has long prided itself on a separation between the army and elected government.

Maoz said that a coup in Israel seemed unimaginable but so did a political assassination until a year ago when a right-wing Jew murdered Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in a bid to halt the Arab-Israeli peace process.
"It is far-fetched, even irresponsible, to take things so far and to assess that such a situation...could lead to a coup," said the daily Maariv newspaper in an editorial on Thursday.
Retired major-general Amram Mitzna agreed but said relations between the government and top officers had reached a boiling point.
"The fact is that there is a growing lack of trust between the military and security echelon and the political echelon... It's an impossible situation," he said.
